about: Emulate round 13 (2026-10-06 18:03 UTC, from the call records), emulate-runs/community-s6c on the laptop: the two v3 runs that read AI in batch 51 (u1 P3+P4a+P5a 0.77, u3 P8-P10 0.99), two calls each, raw outputs exact (balance 239,289 -> 238,627).
u1-emuA:
We don't know for sure what shape the coming fear will take. Some people fear AI because it'll make everyone's life better, some because it'll suck the jobs out from under millions of people, some because it'll interpose itself between us and everything else (and possibly everything else between us and itself), some because all of these. Let's see if the Chantress Seba gets in to any of her applications to communes.

But I can tell you what I want to put my money where. It's better to invest in more human independence than not to. It's better to have community and not need it, than to need it and not have it.

So, when you're designing a community, you have to ask: what connections to the technosphere will you limit, and what ones will you keep?
u1-emuB:
I don't know how much of the fear is accurate, but it's at least possible that AI is going to make life way better for humans and it's also possible that AI is going to suck the jobs out from under millions of people and it's very possible that AI is going to put itself between humans and a lot of stuff they interact with. It's also possible that all of these things are true and I need to hurry up and get my commune applications in with Chantress Seba.

It seems like trying to be more human dependent is a better investment than waiting until I'm sure about what's going on. It'll be better if I have a community and don't need to escape to one than vice versa.

What connections to the technosphere will we limit as we design our community?
u3-emuA:
Medical care is a really tough one. Maybe everyone wants “natural” medical care in the community, but what happens if someone needs trauma surgery, antibiotics, dentistry, obstetric emergency care, or any number of other specialized care? It’s really important to think about how community members will access medical care, what the community will provide through common resources, and what might need to be obtained through outside resources or insurance. It’s also important to discuss how community members will be treated if they choose to be involved with a different level of medical care.

It shouldn’t be necessary for someone in the community to prove their ideological “correctness” when they are scared and sick. If someone in the community becomes catastrophically ill, the community should have already discussed how to support that person to receive the kind of care they choose, using common resources and/or outside resources, while making sure they can access that care and maintain privacy, if they wish. It’s important to remember that the medical care that the community has chosen to participate in may not be enough in a given situation.

It goes without saying that being socially connected is good for one’s health. The Surgeon General’s Advisory on Social Connection lists a number of health outcomes that people who are isolated are more at risk for. While community is not a panacea, it can make a difference in the conditions in which community members get sick, heal from illness, age, and die.
u3-emuB:
Accessing medical care can be a tough nut to crack. What if someone in the community needs trauma surgery, antibiotics, dental care, obstetric care, or some other kind of specialized care? It’s important to discuss in advance how the community is going to help members access medical care, how much the community will contribute from common money to help members access care, whether members will need to acquire outside resources (eg. insurance) to access a certain level of care, and how the community will react to members who want a different level of medical care.

No one should have to prove their ideological colors in a time of need. If a member of the community is severely ill, it is important that the community has discussed in advance how it is going to help the member access the medical care he/she needs, while respecting his/her right to choose the type of medical care he/she wants, help him/her acquire outside resources if necessary, provide transportation to medical appointments, ensure his/her privacy, etc. It’s always good to have a community that can help, because sometimes other means are not enough.

In addition, being connected to a community has measurable health benefits. According to a Surgeon General’s advisory, “social isolation appears to increase the risk for a variety of health outcomes.”
